title: Time reversal symmetry broken quantum spin hall effect in pseudospin-1 Dirac-Rashba system
abstract: The Quantum spin Hall (QSH) phase is conventionally understood to be protected by time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Here, we theoretically investigated the fate of the QSH phase in a pseudospin-1 fermionic $α-\mathcal{T}_3$ system in the presence of a TRS-breaking ferromagnetic exchange field and spin-nonconserving Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Despite broken TRS, the QSH phase survives over a finite parameter regime and is characterised by a non-zero projected spin-Chern number $C_σ(σ= \uparrow, \downarrow)$, protected by a spin-spectral gap. In the absence of Rashba coupling, the QSH phase remains robust up to an $α$-dependent critical exchange field. Rashba SOC qualitatively reshapes the phase diagram by driving transitions into two distinct quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) phases: a $C=2$ phase, irrespective of $α$-values, and a $C=1$ phase for $α\neq 0,1$, which is further identified as a valley-polarized QAH phase arising from a single valley. Rotating the magnetization to in-plane gaps out the first-order helical edge states and gives rise to second-order topological insulator (SOTI) phases that host localized corner states in suitable finite geometry. We further identify a topological phase transition between two different SOTI phases, mediated by nanoribbon edge states at an exchange field equal to $α$. These results establish spin-resolved topology in a higher pseudospin system as well as the $α-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattice as a versatile platform for engineering and controlling multiple topological phases through magnetic exchange and spin-orbit coupling.
summary: This paper theoretically explores the complex interplay between time-reversal symmetry breaking, Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and magnetism in a pseudospin-1 fermionic system. It demonstrates that the QSH phase persists under broken TRS but transitions into distinct QAH phases. Crucially, it also shows how applying an in-plane magnetic field can induce tunable Second-Order Topological Insulator (SOTI) phases hosting localized corner states.
main_problem: The study investigates how the Quantum Spin Hall (QSH) phase survives, transitions, or changes character when Time-Reversal Symmetry (TRS) is broken by a ferromagnetic exchange field and spin mixing occurs via Rashba SOC.
main_result: The system exhibits multiple topological phases, including QSH and distinct Quantum Anomalous Hall (QAH) phases. Furthermore, in-plane magnetization can induce Second-Order Topological Insulator (SOTI) phases with tunable corner states.
method: Theoretical analysis using tight-binding models on the pseudospin-1 $\alpha$-T3 lattice, calculating topological invariants like the spin-Chern number and total Chern number via momentum-space Hamiltonian diagonalization.
model_or_system: The system is a pseudospin-1 fermionic model on an $\alpha$-T3 lattice, incorporating Kane-Mele hopping, Rashba SOC ($\lambda_R$), and ferromagnetic exchange coupling ($\lambda_{ex}$). The Hamiltonian is analyzed in spin-up/spin-down sectors.
key_observables: Spin-Chern number ($C_\sigma$), total Chern number ($C$), bulk band gaps ($\Delta E$), and localized zero-energy corner states (SOTI).
important_parameters: Lattice parameter $\alpha$, Rashba coupling strength ($\lambda_R$), and exchange field strengths ($\lambda_{\perp	ext{ex}}, \lambda_{\parallel	ext{ex}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on projecting the Hamiltonian onto occupied subspaces to define topological invariants when symmetries are broken.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate band structures (e.g., zigzag nanoribbons) showing gap closing/reopening at critical parameter values ($\alpha = \lambda_{	ext{ex}}$), and real-space spectra confirming tunable zero-energy corner modes in SOTI phases.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Hamiltonian's response to broken TRS, first establishing QSH protection, then showing how Rashba SOC drives transitions into specific QAH states, and finally exploring the realization of SOTI phases via in-plane magnetization.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical playground for understanding how multiple topological orders (QSH, QAH, SOTI) can coexist and transition within a single, tunable lattice structure using external magnetic fields and SOC.

The grey region denotes a direct band-gap closing, whereas the blue region indicates closing of the indirect bandgap, both representing a metallic phase.
